It serves as the bridge between ray generation and the actual volume sampling, ensuring that points are generated only within the valid scene bounds and at the correct spatial resolution.

It differs from its parent [Ray-box intersection](776-ray-box-intersection.md) by adding the discretization logic and point generation, and from [Ray Point Sampling](2382-ray-point-sampling.md) by handling the bounding box culling and ray indexing logic explicitly.

Computes the bounding box in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) space from a set of rays.
It calculates the minimum and maximum of ray origins and endpoints in NDC space and returns the stacked min/max bounds.
Computes the near and far clipping distances for ray marching by projecting the 8 corners of the volume bounding box onto the camera view direction.
It extracts the camera position and view direction from the camera matrix (handling world-to-camera vs camera-to-world inversion via a boolean mask to avoid branching).

It generates the 8 corners of the volume in IJK space, transforms them to RAS space using the `ijk2ras` matrix, and projects the vector from the camera to each corner onto the normalized view direction.
The near distance is set to the minimum projected distance minus a margin, and the far distance to the maximum plus the margin.
- **Time Complexity:** $O(N \cdot S)$, where $N$ is the number of rays and $S$ is the average number of samples per ray.
The intersection calculation is $O(N)$, and point generation is $O(N \cdot S)$.
- **Memory Complexity:** $O(N \cdot S)$ to store the generated points, masks, and indices.
- **Strengths:** Ensures samples are only generated within the valid scene volume, reducing unnecessary computations for empty space.
Handles edge cases like zero-direction rays and near-far clipping robustly.
- **When to Use:** When rendering volumetric data within a known bounding box, especially in coarse geometry search phases or when using fixed-step ray marching.
- **When Not to Use:** When the scene geometry is highly irregular and a tight bounding box is not available, or when adaptive step sizes are required for high-frequency details.
This method is a core component of differentiable volume rendering pipelines, particularly those based on Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) or Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) with explicit bounding boxes.
The approach of computing ray-box intersections and then discretizing the intersection interval is a standard technique in computer graphics for ray tracing and volume rendering.
